question: How many pairs of cranial nerves are present in the human body?
explanation: Humans have twelve pairs of cranial nerves that emerge directly from the brain and brainstem. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h1)

question: Which cranial nerve deviates from the general pattern by innervating structures outside the head and neck?
explanation: The vagus nerve travels far beyond the neck region to supply organs within the thoracic and abdominal cavities. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h1)

question: What is the primary function of the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII)?
explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve contains two functional divisions responsible for transmitting auditory signals and equilibrium data from the inner ear. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h2)

question: An anterior skull base fracture that damages the cribriform plate is most likely to affect which cranial nerve?
explanation: The filaments of the olfactory nerve pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, making them vulnerable to shearing forces during anterior skull trauma. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h2)

question: Which cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle to abduct the eyeball?
explanation: The abducens nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle, which pulls the eye outward away from the midline. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h3)

question: A patient with a lower motor neuron lesion of the hypoglossal nerve (XII) will exhibit which physical sign when asked to stick out their tongue?

options.A: Deviation of the tongue toward the healthy side
options.B: Inability to close the mouth or chew food
options.C: Total absence of the gag reflex bilaterally
options.D: Deviation of the tongue toward the affected side

explanation: When the hypoglossal nerve is damaged, the functioning muscle on the normal side pushes the tongue over toward the weak, paralyzed side. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h3)

question: What is the primary motor function of the trigeminal nerve (V)?
explanation: The mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h4)

question: Which cranial nerve provides secretomotor fibers to the lacrimal and submandibular glands, as well as taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
explanation: The facial nerve governs facial expression, anterior tongue taste, and autonomic control of several head glands. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h4)

question: What bedside technique is commonly used to test the motor function of the accessory nerve (XI)?

options.C: Testing visual acuity with a card

explanation: The accessory nerve powers the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles, which are tested by asking the patient to shrug their shoulders against resistance. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h5)

question: A nurse evaluating cranial nerves IX and X together will monitor which physiological response?

options.B: Sensation across the maxillary jaw line
options.C: Elevation of the soft palate and gag reflex

explanation: Cranial nerves IX and X cooperate to innervate the pharynx and soft palate, assessed clinically by checking swallowing, voice quality, and the gag reflex. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h5)

question: Why is corneal protection a primary nursing concern for a patient experiencing acute facial nerve (VII) paralysis?

options.A: The nasolacrimal duct becomes permanently obstructed
options.B: Intraocular pressure increases due to sympathetic overactivity
options.C: The orbicularis oculi muscle cannot close the eyelid fully
options.D: The trigeminal sensory fibers lose all blink sensation

explanation: Facial nerve paralysis weakens the orbicularis oculi, preventing complete eyelid closure and leaving the cornea vulnerable to drying and ulceration. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h6)

question: What is the most critical nursing intervention when caring for a client with impaired swallowing caused by cranial nerve IX and X damage?

options.A: Performing a baseline swallowing screen and keeping suction ready
options.B: Administering strong oral analgesics prior to feeding
options.C: Encouraging high fluid intake with meals
options.D: Positioning the client flat in bed during nutrition delivery

explanation: Dysphagia from lower cranial nerve deficits drastically increases aspiration risk, requiring formal swallow evaluation and emergency suction readiness. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T15#GNS211_U3_T15_h6)
